scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

prediction.raw: This is a complex and emotionally charged situation, and your question touches on **parental boundaries, fairness, and the dynamics of co-parenting**. While there’s no one-size-fits-all answer, here’s a breakdown of the ethical and practical considerations—along with why your instinct to prioritize your scheduled time might be justified, but could also risk escalating conflict. I’ll give you a **0.7/1** (leaning toward **1**, but with caveats). --- ### **Why This Might Be the Right Call (0.7/1)** 1. **You’re Protecting Your Scheduled Time** - Your ex has repeatedly altered the schedule under the guise of "what’s best for the child," often at the expense of your parenting time. This is a classic example of **parental alienation tactics** (not necessarily malicious, but still manipulative). By refusing to give up your scheduled time, you’re enforcing the court-ordered agreement, which is fair to *both* you and your son. - **Key question**: Is your son’s "fun" at the lake or amusement park more important than your *guaranteed* time with him? If the schedule is legally binding, bending it repeatedly sends the message that your time is disposable. 2. **You’re Not Being the "Grumpy" One** - Your ex framed you as unreasonable for being upset about her breaking the schedule. But *she* was the one who: - Cancelled your pickup without notice. - Used your son’s enjoyment as a bargaining chip ("he’s having fun, so you should just wait"). - Made you drive out of your way to retrieve him (a logistical burden). - **Power dynamics matter**: If she’s consistently making demands that inconvenience you, it’s okay to push back—especially when it’s not about the child’s well-being but her own preferences. 3. **You’re Modeling Boundaries for Your Son** - Children thrive on consistency. If they see one parent constantly giving in to the other’s whims, it can create confusion or resentment. By standing firm, you’re teaching your son that his time with *both* parents is valuable and predictable. 4. **The "Make-Up Time" Argument** - You’re not asking for extra time; you’re asking for the time *you’re owed*. If she’s been flexible in the past (even if it was to her advantage), it’s time to call it even. The 4th of July party is her family’s event—it’s not your responsibility to accommodate it at the cost of your scheduled parenting time. --- ### **Why This Could Be Problematic (Why Not a 1/1)** 1. **Escalating Conflict** - If you keep this up, your ex may: - **Refuse to return your son** at all (even if temporarily), using your son as leverage. - **File a complaint** with child services or the court, framing you as the "uncooperative" parent. - **Withdraw further cooperation**, making co-parenting even harder. - **Risk**: You might win this battle but lose the long-term relationship with your son (or the ability to see him at all). 2. **The "Best Interest of the Child" Test** - Courts and mediators prioritize what’s *actually* in the child’s best interest, not just your feelings. Ask yourself: - Is your son *truly* having a better time with her family than he would with you? - Are you missing out on something meaningful with him (e.g., a shared activity, quality time) because of this? - If you keep your son, will he feel "punished" for her family’s plans? (Even if unintentionally.) - **Alternative approach**: Could you compromise? For example: - "I’ll pick him up after the lake trip, but we’ll do something special together tomorrow to make up for it." - "I’ll attend the 4th of July party for an hour, then take him home to spend the rest of the day with me." 3. **The "Slippery Slope"** - If you start refusing to give up your scheduled time *every* time she asks, she may: - **Stop inviting you to events** (which could feel like exclusion). - **Use your son as a pawn** in future disputes (e.g., "Dad won’t let me see him, so I’m not letting you either"). - **Better strategy**: Be firm *this time* (since she broke the agreement), but leave room for flexibility in the future if she genuinely has a valid reason (e.g., your son is sick). 4. **Your Son’s Perspective** - At 8 years old, your son is old enough to understand routines. If he’s used to his mom’s family trips happening on your weekend, he might feel confused or upset when you suddenly change the plan. - **Question**: Does he *want* to go to the amusement park with her, or is he going because she’s making the rules? If it’s the latter, he might resent you for "ruining his fun." --- ### **What You Could Do Instead (A Middle Ground)** 1. **Document Everything** - Save texts, emails, and any evidence of her breaking the schedule. If she continues to do this, you may need to go back to court to enforce the agreement. 2. **Propose a Compromise** - Example: *"I understand you want to take him to the lake, but since it’s on my weekend, I’d like to adjust the schedule so we can do something special together tomorrow. How about we switch weekends next time so you can have your lake trip?"* - This keeps the door open for future flexibility while protecting your time. 3. **Set a Boundary for the Future** - Next time she asks to move your scheduled time, respond with: *"I appreciate the thought, but our court-ordered schedule is in place for a reason. If it’s truly necessary, we can discuss adjusting it in advance—but I can’t guarantee I’ll be able to accommodate last-minute changes."* 4. **Focus on Quality Time** - Instead of fighting over quantity, make your time with him *exceptional*. Plan activities he loves, and he may be less likely to want to spend time elsewhere. 5. **Consider Mediation** - If this keeps happening, a neutral mediator could help restructure the schedule to be more fair (e.g., adding a midweek day or extending weekends). --- ### **Final Verdict: 0.7/1 (But With Conditions)** You’re **not the asshole** for prioritizing your scheduled time—especially after years of her bending the rules. However, **how you handle this moving forward** will determine whether you escalate conflict or find a sustainable solution. **If you keep your son this weekend:** - **Pros**: You enforce the schedule, send a message that your time matters, and avoid being taken advantage of. - **Cons**: Risk of backlash, potential long-term co-parenting breakdown, and your son might feel caught in the middle. **If you compromise (e.g., pick him up after the lake trip):** - **Pros**: Preserves the relationship with your ex, keeps your son happy, and avoids a power struggle. - **Cons**: You might still feel like you’re being shortchanged. **Best Approach**: - **This weekend**: Keep your son during your scheduled time (since she broke the agreement). But **do it calmly**—avoid saying things like "I told you so" or making her feel guilty. Frame it as: *"I’m sorry, but our schedule is set, and I need to follow it."* - **Moving forward**: Propose a **revised schedule** that’s fairer for both of you (e.g., adding a midweek day). If she refuses, go back to court to modify the agreement. --- ### **Key Takeaway** You’re not wrong for feeling frustrated—**this is a common issue in co-parenting**. The goal isn’t to "win" but to **protect your relationship with your son** while ensuring you’re treated fairly. If she continues to manipulate the schedule, you may need legal intervention, but for now, **standing your ground is reasonable**. Would you like help drafting a text to her to explain your stance without escalating things?
